newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Sumitomo copper business seen retrenching.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sumitomo copper business seen retrenching.

text.p: A sharp fall in copper sales by scandal-hit Sumitomo Corp in the first half of the 1996/97 business year is a clear sign of the Japanese trader's pull-back in the Asian copper market, traders said on Tuesday.
"We've heard from the consumer side that Sumitomo are reducing their supply across the board," the head of one metal broker's trading desk in Singapore said.

"They may try and hold on to some markets like Taiwan, but it's no surprise they've curtailed their active trade. They've got less physical inventories and the volume of tonnage available for long-term contracts is less," he added.

Sumitomo announced in Tokyo on Tuesday that its refined copper sales in the first half of the 1996/97 business year ending in March plunged to $181.2 billion yen ($1.63 billion), down by 57 percent or $243.3 billion yen ($2.19 billion) versus the same period of the previous year.

"Since (former chief trader) Hamanaka was dismissed in June, we've being handling only necessary copper business such as long term contracts," Sumitomo executive vice-president Takehiko Yonezu told reporters.
"We have no plan to withdraw from the copper business at the moment, but are working out future strategy at the non-ferrous metal department," Yonezu said.
Before Sumitomo fired him in mid-June of this year, Yasuo Hamanaka was considered the most influential and controversial player in the world copper market.
It has blamed Hamanaka for racking up estimated losses of $2.6 billion from unauthorised copper trading, and this has been called the world's biggest-ever loss on financial markets.
Hamanaka was recently arrested on suspicion of fraud and forgery in connection with those trades.

Metal traders have said Hamanaka used profits generated by his copper futures trading on the London Metal Exchange (LME) to offset cut-price sales to win market share in the Asian physical copper market.
But one major Japanese copper user, however, countered, that Sumitomo was offering copper at only marginally lower prices than its competitors were.
Hamanaka's advantages derived from the quicker, more reliable delivery made possible by selling from his own stocks, the user said.
Industry sources said there were already signs that Sumitomo was preparing to surrender market share in some countries.

But the head of Sumitomo Corp's operations in Singapore told Reuters that the company did not intend to withdraw from Asian physical copper markets, although it might not be as competitive on pricing as before.

"It is not our intention to withdraw, but our approach might be slightly different...Our new offer prices may not be as competitive as before," said Hisayoshi Uno, managing director of Sumitomo Corp Singapore Pte Ltd.

Sompong Nakorsri, the chief executive officer of major Thai copper buyer Bangkok Cable Co., told Reuters in Tokyo that Sumitomo was preparing to pull out of Thailand's refined copper trade entirely next year.

"Sumitomo doesn't look to supply any copper cathode in Thailand next year," he said. In a telephone interview, Sompong said Sumitomo had supplied more than 40 percent of Thailand's copper cathode market.
Local industry sources expect Thailand's demand for refined copper to reach nearly 200,000 tonnes this year.
An official for Sumitomo's copper division in Taipei confirmed that Sumitomo was planning to restructure its copper business in Asia.
The company might pull out of Thailand, but its Taiwan operation would not be affected, she said.
Malaysian cable makers also said they were prepared for a halt in refined copper supplies from Sumitomo next year.
However, the trader only supplied between 10 and 15 percent of the country's consumption of about 160,000 tonnes of copper cathode a year.
